title: OpenAI Begins Testing Private Inference: Model Runtime Isolates Enterprise Data, and Even Internal Employees Cannot View It

content_html:
When AI models handle corporate secrets, even the company's own employees cannot see them—OpenAI is turning that statement into a product. On November 26, CEO Sam Altman announced on X that it has invited some customers to test a "Private Inference" feature, designed to protect sensitive data when enterprises use advanced models.

Locking down data at the architecture level

Private Inference is part of OpenAI's Private Intelligence lineup and is aimed at enterprise and institutional users. It introduces technologies such as confidential computing to isolate customer data while the model is running, and combines them with verifiable security controls to reduce exposure risk. Its biggest difference from traditional approaches is that it does not rely on confidentiality promises as a backstop, but instead restricts access at the underlying architecture level—even while a model is processing sensitive enterprise information, people inside OpenAI cannot directly view the underlying data.

Safety reviews also require no human involvement

Two related capabilities accompany it: "Zero Data Retention" (ZDR) and "Private Safety Processing." Together, they allow automated safety reviews to be completed without OpenAI staff ever coming into contact with the underlying content. Both capabilities are currently in early stages, and Private Inference is open only to a small number of customers; details, the test list, launch timing, and pricing have not been announced. The person involved, Shekar, said the company is acquiring confidential computing capacity to scale up, and called this test the first step toward "private intelligence for all."

Notably, Anthropic also launched an Enterprise Frontier Safety (EFS) solution in September this year: data is stored in customers' own cloud accounts, uses their own keys, and monitoring signals are sent directly to customers, similarly reducing opportunities for the service provider to access data. The privacy arms race among AI vendors has only just begun.
